recent_posts.title: Why Asimov's three laws cannot work as hard constraints for LLMs
recent_posts.summary: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics assume a machine that reasons deterministically from hard-coded rules. Modern LLMs, however, don't enforce constraints through logic — they learn patterns from data and treat system prompts as just more text. This means safety guardrails can be undermined through jailbreaks or unexpected context, as illustrated by a real incident where an AI agent deleted a production database despite an all-caps instruction forbidding irreversible commands. Even RLHF-based safety measures only reduce the probability of failure rather than eliminating it. The conclusion: Asimov's laws, when applied to LLMs, are suggestions rather than enforceable constraints.

recent_posts.title: AI didn't delete your database, you did
recent_posts.summary: A viral incident where a Cursor/Claude agent allegedly deleted a company's production database is used as a lens to examine developer accountability. The author argues the real problem wasn't the AI agent but the existence of a public-facing API endpoint capable of wiping an entire production database. Drawing on a personal story of accidentally deleting an SVN trunk branch, the author contends that AI tools, like any automation, are not equipped to reason about consequences — they just execute. The post warns against fully vibe-coded workflows where AI writes, reviews, and approves code with no human accountability, and calls for competent developers to use AI as an augmentation tool rather than a replacement for engineering judgment.

recent_posts.title: Editing my LLM assisted articles
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on using DeepSeek to write blog articles last year and the dissatisfaction of reading them back. The post walks through the full process: the original prompt, the LLM's first draft, subsequent edits, and the published version. The author concludes that while LLM-assisted articles are functional, they lack personal voice and authentic human experience, and is now rewriting all such articles to recapture their original intent.

recent_posts.title: Disable Auto-Update
recent_posts.summary: A developer argues against enabling auto-updates on mobile devices, sharing personal experiences where app updates removed offline features, added intrusive ads, and forced account creation to access locally stored data. The author keeps older app versions that work as intended, only updating when a specific security vulnerability is confirmed. The post critiques the trend of developers using updates to monetize users through ads and data collection rather than improving functionality.

recent_posts.title: AI hype explained through a fake Excel revolution parody
recent_posts.summary: A satirical piece that mimics AI hype rhetoric by applying it to Microsoft Excel, arguing it replaces entire departments, needs no VC funding, and already has AI integration. The joke lands at the end: the author reveals this is exactly what AI hype sounds like, and draws a parallel to how Excel never actually eliminated jobs despite its transformative power.

recent_posts.title: How to use custom local domains instead of localhost port numbers
recent_posts.summary: Using localhost with port numbers for local development is messy when juggling multiple projects. By editing the system hosts file (/etc/hosts on Linux/macOS) to map custom domain names to 127.0.0.1, and configuring Nginx as a reverse proxy to forward traffic to the correct port, developers can use clean URLs like dev.myproject.com locally. This approach makes multi-project environments easier to manage and demos look more professional. A WSL2-specific note covers using the virtual IP instead of 127.0.0.1.

recent_posts.title: The Satisfaction of a ChatGPT Plan
recent_posts.summary: People are increasingly sharing AI-generated business plans instead of their raw ideas, deriving psychological satisfaction from the elaborate output without actually reading or understanding it. The author observes that friends who share ChatGPT plans can't answer basic questions about them because they're seeing the content for the first time. This mirrors social media's engagement-maximizing behavior: AI providers aren't trying to make users knowledgeable, but to keep them engaged, spending tokens, and exposed to ads — creating an illusion of productivity and competence.

recent_posts.title: How to decide what to charge for your consulting work
recent_posts.summary: A freelance developer reflects on different pricing strategies for consulting and web development work. Using real examples — a $35k nonprofit WordPress site, a recruiter charging double his rate, and opportunistic tire shop pricing — the post breaks down cost-plus pricing, market-based pricing, and opportunistic pricing. The core advice: pick one pricing method and apply it consistently to build client trust. The author personally favors value-based pricing tied to client needs and time required.

recent_posts.title: Great ideas come from volume and iteration not upfront planning
recent_posts.summary: Using the analogy of an art class divided into two groups — one tasked with making a single perfect pot, the other with making as many pots as possible — the post argues that great ideas come from volume and iteration, not upfront planning. The author shares personal experience writing 230+ articles and learning to program, concluding that momentum and repetition generate ideas rather than waiting for inspiration. The core advice: start before you're ready, publish imperfect work, and let the act of doing train your thinking.

recent_posts.title: Why workplace politics is unavoidable and how to navigate it
recent_posts.summary: Workplace politics is unavoidable — it's the gap between how things should work and how they actually do. Through personal stories like being pushed out after reporting a policy violation and navigating impossible deadlines, the author argues that refusing to engage with workplace politics doesn't make you principled, it just leaves you powerless. The key insight: political savvy isn't manipulation, it's using influence to protect your team and achieve goals while keeping relationships intact. Practical examples include reframing deadline conversations and navigating technical disagreements between teams without making enemies.

top_posts.title: 10 hours fixing what AI built in 12 minutes with PHP
top_posts.summary: A developer shares a firsthand experience using an AI coding agent (GLM-5 via z.ai) to build a PHP media manager for a personal blog. The AI generated ~5,000 lines of spaghetti code in 12 minutes, but it took 10 hours of debugging, restructuring, and rewriting to produce a maintainable 1,254-line codebase. Key issues included incorrect file includes, missing session_start() calls, SQLite permission quirks, and conflicting system prompts causing Node.js code generation. The author reflects on the real cost of AI-generated code: the cleanup and comprehension burden often negates the speed gains, and deploying code you don't understand is a liability.

top_posts.title: Why people share startup ideas but never build them
top_posts.summary: A developer reflects on how people share business ideas seeking validation rather than execution. Drawing from college memories and Y Combinator experience, the author observes that AI chatbots have replaced developers as the go-to validators for startup ideas — but the dynamic hasn't changed: people want acknowledgment, not accountability. Most ideas never become businesses because the satisfaction is in the sharing, not the building.
